paragraphs.heading: Resin turned fossil
paragraphs.text: Amber is resin from trees that has become a fossil. People have admired its colors, orange, brown and now and then red, since Neolithic times, and craftsmen have shaped it as a gem since classical antiquity. Today it goes into jewelry, and folk medicine has treated it as a cure. Experts count more than 150 types of amber, sorted into five classes by the chemicals they contain.

paragraphs.heading: Life caught inside
paragraphs.text: Resin starts out soft and sticky, so pieces of animals and plants sometimes get stuck in it and end up sealed inside the amber. These trapped bits are called inclusions. Other things mixed into the resin can change its color: pyrites, for example, can give it a bluish look. Cloudy "bony" amber gets its milky look from huge numbers of tiny bubbles. Even in dark or opaque amber, scientists can image the inclusions with powerful, high-resolution X-rays.

paragraphs.heading: What it is made of
paragraphs.text: Amber is not one pure substance but a mix of several resins, some of which dissolve in alcohol, ether or chloroform, plus a part that does not dissolve. Chemically it is a macromolecule, a single giant molecule built when smaller terpenoid building blocks join together. Over time it matures as more links form and its molecules rearrange, cross-link and close into rings, which gives amber its stable fossil structure. Most amber rates between 2.0 and 2.5 on the Mohs hardness scale, with a specific gravity of 1.06 to 1.10. Heated above 200 °C it breaks down into oil of amber and a black leftover, which can be dissolved in turpentine or linseed oil to make amber varnish.

paragraphs.heading: A name borrowed from whales
paragraphs.text: The English word amber first meant ambergris, a waxy solid that comes from the sperm whale. In the Romance languages the name spread to fossil resin from the Baltic by the late 13th century, and English picked up that meaning by the early 15th century. As ambergris fell out of use, the resin became what amber usually means. The two may have been mixed up because both were found washed up on beaches. They behave differently in water, though: ambergris floats, while amber sinks unless the water is very salty.

paragraphs.heading: The stone behind electricity
paragraphs.text: In Ancient Greek, amber was called elektron. Because amber can hold a charge of static electricity, that word gave English electric and electricity. It holds the charge because it insulates well, so electrons cannot travel from its surface through the material. One account describes women in Syria who made the whorls of their spindles from amber and named it harpax, since it pulled leaves, chaff and light threads toward it.

paragraphs.heading: The Amber Road and beyond
paragraphs.text: Amber moved along long trade routes. A network known as the Amber Road joined the Baltic Sea to the Mediterranean. The Romans were buying amber from the southern Baltic shores at least as early as the reign of Nero. China also has its own long history with amber, starting with a written record from 200 BCE.
